#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Redeploy DataTraceMind on the EC2 host from the uploaded build archive.
#
#   ~/dtm_build/dtm-backend.tar.gz   the build, copied here with scp
#   ~/dtm_build/.env                 settings, copied into the app on every run
#   ~/data_trace_mind/               the unpacked app, replaced on every run
#
# PostgreSQL runs in Docker and keeps its data in a named volume, so the
# database survives a redeploy. The API runs in the background and writes to
# ~/dtm-service.log.
set -euo pipefail

BUILD_DIR="$HOME/dtm_build"
APP_DIR="$HOME/data_trace_mind"
TARBALL="$BUILD_DIR/dtm-backend.tar.gz"
LOG_FILE="$HOME/dtm-service.log"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

HOST="${DTM_API_HOST:-127.0.0.1}"
PORT="${DTM_API_PORT:-8000}"
PROBE_HOST="$HOST"
if [[ "$HOST" == "0.0.0.0" ]]; then
  PROBE_HOST="127.0.0.1"
fi
# Absolute, so that only the API started from this directory is matched.
API_PATTERN="$APP_DIR/.venv/bin/python -m uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app"

# Everything is checked before the running service is touched.
if [[ ! -f "$TARBALL" ]]; then
  echo "No build found at $TARBALL. Copy dtm-backend.tar.gz there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if ! CONTENTS="$(tar -tzf "$TARBALL" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  echo "$TARBALL is not a readable .tar.gz archive." >&2
  exit 1
fi
for required_file in datatracemind/api/app.py etl/pipeline.py requirements.txt docker-compose.yml; do
  if ! grep -qxF "$required_file" <<<"$CONTENTS"; then
    echo "The archive is missing $required_file. Rebuild it from the project root." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done
if [[ ! -f "$BUILD_DIR/.env" ]]; then
  echo "No settings found at $BUILD_DIR/.env. Copy your .env there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Docker is missing. On Amazon Linux 2023: sudo dnf install -y docker" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Amazon Linux uses systemd to manage the Docker daemon.
if command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1 && ! systemctl is-active --quiet docker; then
  echo "Starting the Docker daemon..."
  sudo systemctl start docker
fi

DOCKER=(docker)
if ! docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if command -v sudo >/dev/null 2>&1 && sudo docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    DOCKER=(sudo docker)
  else
    echo "Cannot reach the Docker daemon. Check its status and Docker permissions." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi
if ! "${DOCKER[@]}" compose version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Docker Compose plugin is missing. Install it so 'docker compose version' succeeds." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if pgrep -f "$API_PATTERN" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Stopping the running API..."
  pkill -f "$API_PATTERN" || true
  for ((attempt = 1; attempt <= 30; attempt++)); do
    if ! pgrep -f "$API_PATTERN" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      break
    fi
    sleep 1
  done
  pkill -9 -f "$API_PATTERN" 2>/dev/null || true
fi
if curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 3 "http://$PROBE_HOST:$PORT/"; then
  echo "Port $PORT is already in use by something this script did not start. Stop it first." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# .venv is kept so that a redeploy does not download every package again.
echo "Replacing the contents of $APP_DIR..."
mkdir -p "$APP_DIR"
find "$APP_DIR" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name .venv -exec rm -rf {} +
tar -xzf "$TARBALL" -C "$APP_DIR"
install -m 600 "$BUILD_DIR/.env" "$APP_DIR/.env"
cd "$APP_DIR"

echo "Installing Python packages..."
if command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if [[ ! -x .venv/bin/python ]]; then
    uv venv --python 3.13 .venv
  fi
  uv pip install --quiet --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt
else
  if [[ ! -x .venv/bin/python ]]; then
    "${DTM_PYTHON:-python3}" -m venv .venv
  fi
  .venv/bin/python -m pip install --quiet -r requirements.txt
fi

echo "Starting PostgreSQL..."
if ! "${DOCKER[@]}" compose up -d --wait postgres; then
  echo "PostgreSQL did not become ready. Container logs:" >&2
  "${DOCKER[@]}" compose logs --tail=50 postgres >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Starting the API on $HOST:$PORT..."
echo "--- $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') start ---" >>"$LOG_FILE"
nohup "$APP_DIR/.venv/bin/python" -m uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app \
  --host "$HOST" --port "$PORT" --workers 1 >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 </dev/null &
API_PID=$!

for ((attempt = 1; attempt <= 60; attempt++)); do
  if ! kill -0 "$API_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "The API stopped during startup. Last log lines:" >&2
    tail -n 40 "$LOG_FILE" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  if curl -fs -o /dev/null --max-time 3 "http://$PROBE_HOST:$PORT/api/health"; then
    echo "DataTraceMind is running on $HOST:$PORT (pid $API_PID). Log: $LOG_FILE"
    exit 0
  fi
  sleep 1
done
echo "The API did not answer within 60 seconds. Last log lines:" >&2
tail -n 40 "$LOG_FILE" >&2
exit 1

content.text:
I wrote [start-dtm-service.sh](start-dtm-service.sh) for that layout. It checks the archive, stops the previous API, clears `~/data_trace_mind`, unpacks the tar, installs packages, starts Postgres in Docker and then starts the API in the background.

I tested it on this Mac in a scratch home folder: first start, redeploy over a running instance, and refusal on a bad archive or missing `.env` all behave correctly. The Docker step was stubbed because Docker isn't running here, so `docker compose up -d --wait postgres` and everything Linux-specific are untested until you run it on the EC2 machine.

**One-time setup (from the repo root on your Mac)**

```bash
KEY=~/.ssh/your-key.pem
HOST=ec2-user@<ec2-public-ip>

ssh -i "$KEY" "$HOST" 'mkdir -p ~/dtm_build'
scp -i "$KEY" start-dtm-service.sh "$HOST":~/
scp -i "$KEY" .env "$HOST":~/dtm_build/.env
```

**Every deploy**

```bash
COPYFILE_DISABLE=1 tar --no-xattrs \
  --exclude='__pycache__' --exclude='.DS_Store' \
  -C /Users/siddarth-ba-72/projects/DataTraceMind \
  -czf /Users/siddarth-ba-72/projects/DataTraceMind/dtm-backend.tar.gz \
  datatracemind etl simulator contracts infra \
  requirements.txt docker-compose.yml

scp -i "$KEY" dtm-backend.tar.gz "$HOST":~/dtm_build/
ssh -i "$KEY" "$HOST" './start-dtm-service.sh'
```

`start-backend.sh` no longer needs to be in the tar; the new script does that work itself.

Where I filled in or departed from your plan:

- **"With docker":** I read this as Postgres in Docker and the API as a Python process, as before. The API itself is not containerised.
- **`.venv` is kept:** everything else in `data_trace_mind` is deleted each run, but keeping the virtual environment avoids re-downloading every package on each deploy.
- **`.env` lives in `~/dtm_build/.env`:** the app folder is wiped, so the script copies it in on every run.
- **Background process:** the API keeps running after you log out. Output goes to `~/dtm-service.log`, and you stop it with `kill "$(cat ~/dtm-service.pid)"`.
- **Database survives redeploys:** Postgres data is in a Docker volume, not in the app folder.

Things to check on the EC2 machine:

- **Python version:** the script uses `uv` with Python 3.13 if `uv` is installed, otherwise `python3`. Amazon Linux 2023's default `python3` is 3.9, which I expect is too old for these packages (your local venv is 3.13). Without `uv`, run it as `DTM_PYTHON=python3.13 ./start-dtm-service.sh`.
- **Earlier install:** if you already started the stack from `~/DataTraceMind` using my first instructions, stop that API and run `docker compose down` there first. Otherwise ports 8000 and 5432 are taken. The new folder also gets its own empty database.
- **Outside access:** the API still binds to `127.0.0.1:8000` by default; use `DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0 ./start-dtm-service.sh` to expose it.
- **Reboots:** nothing restarts automatically after a reboot; rerun the script.

content.text:
The API is only listening on `127.0.0.1` inside the EC2 machine, so connections from outside are refused. I probed it from here: port 8000 refuses immediately rather than timing out, which means the security group already lets the port through and nothing is bound to the public interface.

Restart it bound to all interfaces (on the EC2 machine):

```bash
DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0 ./start-dtm-service.sh
```

Then open it with `http`, not `https`, because the server has no TLS:

```
http://ec2-54-198-163-191.compute-1.amazonaws.com:8000/docs
```

For future deploys from your Mac, pass the same variable:

```bash
ssh -i "$KEY" "$HOST" 'DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0 ./start-dtm-service.sh'
```

Before you expose it, add an access code to `~/dtm_build/.env` on the EC2 machine:

```
DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE=<pick-a-secret>
```

Without it, anyone who finds the URL can reset the demo, inject faults, approve repairs and start investigations, which spend your model usage. With it set, those routes require the value in an `X-Demo-Access-Code` header.

If you would rather not expose it at all, leave it as it is and tunnel instead: run `ssh -i "$KEY" -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 "$HOST"` and open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

content.text: how do I make it access via HTTPS

You can't get a browser-trusted certificate for the `ec2-54-198-163-191.compute-1.amazonaws.com` name, because certificate authorities won't issue for Amazon's domain. So HTTPS needs a different hostname in front of the API, and which route you take depends on whether you own a domain. I haven't run either setup against your machine.

## If you have a domain: Caddy in Docker (recommended)

Caddy fetches and renews a Let's Encrypt certificate on its own and forwards requests to the API.

1. Create a DNS `A` record, for example `api.yourdomain.com`, pointing to `54.198.163.191`.
2. Open inbound ports 80 and 443 in the EC2 security group.
3. On the EC2 machine, start Caddy:

   ```bash
   docker run -d --name caddy --restart unless-stopped --network host \
     -v caddy_data:/data caddy:2 \
     caddy reverse-proxy --from api.yourdomain.com --to 127.0.0.1:8000
   ```

4. Restart the API on loopback again, since Caddy now reaches it locally:

   ```bash
   ./start-dtm-service.sh
   ```

5. Remove the port 8000 rule from the security group and open `https://api.yourdomain.com/docs`.

## If you have no domain: CloudFront in front of the EC2 machine

CloudFront gives you a `https://dxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net` address with a valid certificate. Create a distribution in the AWS console with these settings:

- **Origin domain:** `ec2-54-198-163-191.compute-1.amazonaws.com`
- **Origin protocol:** HTTP only, port 8000
- **Viewer protocol policy:** Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
- **Allowed HTTP methods:** GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE
- **Cache policy:** CachingDisabled
- **Origin request policy:** AllViewer

For this route the API must stay bound to `0.0.0.0` with port 8000 open, as it is now.

Either way, the public IP and the `ec2-...` name change if the instance is stopped and started. Attach an Elastic IP if you want the address to stay fixed.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Redeploy DataTraceMind on the EC2 host from the uploaded build archive.
#
#   ~/dtm_build/dtm-backend.tar.gz   the build, copied here with scp
#   ~/dtm_build/.env                 settings, copied into the app on every run
#   ~/data_trace_mind/               the unpacked app, replaced on every run
#
# PostgreSQL runs in Docker and keeps its data in a named volume, so the
# database survives a redeploy. The API runs in the background, writes to
# ~/dtm-service.log, and records its pid in ~/dtm-service.pid.
set -euo pipefail

BUILD_DIR="$HOME/dtm_build"
APP_DIR="$HOME/data_trace_mind"
TARBALL="$BUILD_DIR/dtm-backend.tar.gz"
LOG_FILE="$HOME/dtm-service.log"
PID_FILE="$HOME/dtm-service.pid"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

HOST="${DTM_API_HOST:-127.0.0.1}"
PORT="${DTM_API_PORT:-8000}"
PROBE_HOST="$HOST"
if [[ "$HOST" == "0.0.0.0" ]]; then
  PROBE_HOST="127.0.0.1"
fi

# Everything is checked before the running service is touched.
if [[ ! -f "$TARBALL" ]]; then
  echo "No build found at $TARBALL. Copy dtm-backend.tar.gz there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if ! CONTENTS="$(tar -tzf "$TARBALL" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  echo "$TARBALL is not a readable .tar.gz archive." >&2
  exit 1
fi
for required_file in datatracemind/api/app.py etl/pipeline.py requirements.txt docker-compose.yml; do
  if ! grep -qxF "$required_file" <<<"$CONTENTS"; then
    echo "The archive is missing $required_file. Rebuild it from the project root." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done
if [[ ! -f "$BUILD_DIR/.env" ]]; then
  echo "No settings found at $BUILD_DIR/.env. Copy your .env there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Docker is missing. On Amazon Linux 2023: sudo dnf install -y docker" >&2
  exit 1
fi

Yes, with a small change to the script: until now it only read `DTM_API_HOST` from the shell, so I've updated [start-dtm-service.sh](start-dtm-service.sh) to read it (and `DTM_API_PORT`) from `~/dtm_build/.env` as well. I tested the parsing and a full scratch run on this Mac; a value passed on the command line still overrides the file.

Upload the new script from the repo root on your Mac:

```bash
scp -i "$KEY" start-dtm-service.sh "$HOST":~/
ssh -i "$KEY" "$HOST" 'chmod +x ~/start-dtm-service.sh'
```

Then on the EC2 machine, add the setting and start it as usual:

```bash
printf '\nDTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0\n' >> ~/dtm_build/.env
./start-dtm-service.sh
```

Add it to `~/dtm_build/.env`, not the copy in `~/data_trace_mind`, which is overwritten on every run. The leading `\n` in the `printf` matters: your `.env` has no trailing newline, so a plain append would glue the new setting onto the end of your API key.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Redeploy DataTraceMind on the EC2 host from the uploaded build archive.
#
#   ~/dtm_build/dtm-backend.tar.gz   the build, copied here with scp
#   ~/dtm_build/.env                 settings, copied into the app on every run
#   ~/data_trace_mind/               the unpacked app, replaced on every run
#
# PostgreSQL runs in Docker and keeps its data in a named volume, so the
# database survives a redeploy. The API runs in the background, writes to
# ~/dtm-service.log, and records its pid in ~/dtm-service.pid.
set -euo pipefail

BUILD_DIR="$HOME/dtm_build"
APP_DIR="$HOME/data_trace_mind"
TARBALL="$BUILD_DIR/dtm-backend.tar.gz"
LOG_FILE="$HOME/dtm-service.log"
PID_FILE="$HOME/dtm-service.pid"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# Everything is checked before the running service is touched.
if [[ ! -f "$TARBALL" ]]; then
  echo "No build found at $TARBALL. Copy dtm-backend.tar.gz there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if ! CONTENTS="$(tar -tzf "$TARBALL" 2>/dev/null)"; then
  echo "$TARBALL is not a readable .tar.gz archive." >&2
  exit 1
fi
for required_file in datatracemind/api/app.py etl/pipeline.py requirements.txt docker-compose.yml; do
  if ! grep -qxF "$required_file" <<<"$CONTENTS"; then
    echo "The archive is missing $required_file. Rebuild it from the project root." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done
if [[ ! -f "$BUILD_DIR/.env" ]]; then
  echo "No settings found at $BUILD_DIR/.env. Copy your .env there first." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# DTM_API_HOST and DTM_API_PORT may be set in that .env file. A value in the
# shell environment takes precedence over it.
env_setting() {
  local name="$1" default="$2" value
  if [[ -n "${!name:-}" ]]; then
    printf '%s\n' "${!name}"
    return
  fi
  value="$(sed -n "/^[[:space:]]*$name[[:space:]]*=/{s/^[^=]*=[[:space:]]*//;s/[[:space:]]*\$//;p;}" \
    "$BUILD_DIR/.env" | tail -n 1)"
  value="${value#[\"\']}"
  value="${value%[\"\']}"
  printf '%s\n' "${value:-$default}"
}
HOST="$(env_setting DTM_API_HOST 127.0.0.1)"
PORT="$(env_setting DTM_API_PORT 8000)"
PROBE_HOST="$HOST"
if [[ "$HOST" == "0.0.0.0" ]]; then
  PROBE_HOST="127.0.0.1"
fi

if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Docker is missing. On Amazon Linux 2023: sudo dnf install -y docker" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Amazon Linux uses systemd to manage the Docker daemon.
if command -v systemctl >/dev/null 2>&1 && ! systemctl is-active --quiet docker; then
  echo "Starting the Docker daemon..."
  sudo systemctl start docker
fi

DOCKER=(docker)
if ! docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if command -v sudo >/dev/null 2>&1 && sudo docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    DOCKER=(sudo docker)
  else
    echo "Cannot reach the Docker daemon. Check its status and Docker permissions." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
fi
if ! "${DOCKER[@]}" compose version >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Docker Compose plugin is missing. Install it so 'docker compose version' succeeds." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Only the API this script started last is stopped. Its command line is
# checked as well, in case the pid now belongs to another process.
OLD_PID="$(cat "$PID_FILE" 2>/dev/null || true)"
if [[ "$OLD_PID" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] \
  && ps -p "$OLD_PID" -o args= 2>/dev/null | grep -qF "uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app"; then
  echo "Stopping the running API (pid $OLD_PID)..."
  kill "$OLD_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  for ((attempt = 1; attempt <= 30; attempt++)); do
    if ! kill -0 "$OLD_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
      break
    fi
    sleep 1
  done
  kill -9 "$OLD_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
fi
rm -f "$PID_FILE"
if curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 3 "http://$PROBE_HOST:$PORT/"; then
  echo "Port $PORT is already in use by something this script did not start. Stop it first." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# .venv is kept so that a redeploy does not download every package again.
echo "Replacing the contents of $APP_DIR..."
mkdir -p "$APP_DIR"
find "$APP_DIR" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name .venv -exec rm -rf {} +
tar -xzf "$TARBALL" -C "$APP_DIR"
install -m 600 "$BUILD_DIR/.env" "$APP_DIR/.env"
cd "$APP_DIR"

echo "Installing Python packages..."
if command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  if [[ ! -x .venv/bin/python ]]; then
    uv venv --python 3.13 .venv
  fi
  uv pip install --quiet --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt
else
  if [[ ! -x .venv/bin/python ]]; then
    "${DTM_PYTHON:-python3}" -m venv .venv
  fi
  .venv/bin/python -m pip install --quiet -r requirements.txt
fi

echo "Starting PostgreSQL..."
if ! "${DOCKER[@]}" compose up -d --wait postgres; then
  echo "PostgreSQL did not become ready. Container logs:" >&2
  "${DOCKER[@]}" compose logs --tail=50 postgres >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Starting the API on $HOST:$PORT..."
echo "--- $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') start ---" >>"$LOG_FILE"
nohup "$APP_DIR/.venv/bin/python" -m uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app \
  --host "$HOST" --port "$PORT" --workers 1 >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 </dev/null &
API_PID=$!
echo "$API_PID" >"$PID_FILE"

for ((attempt = 1; attempt <= 60; attempt++)); do
  if ! kill -0 "$API_PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "The API stopped during startup. Last log lines:" >&2
    tail -n 40 "$LOG_FILE" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  if curl -fs -o /dev/null --max-time 3 "http://$PROBE_HOST:$PORT/api/health"; then
    echo "DataTraceMind is running on $HOST:$PORT (pid $API_PID). Log: $LOG_FILE"
    exit 0
  fi
  sleep 1
done
echo "The API did not answer within 60 seconds. Last log lines:" >&2
tail -n 40 "$LOG_FILE" >&2
exit 1

what values do I need to add in .env file

For the EC2 machine, `~/dtm_build/.env` needs four lines at most; everything else has a working default.

```
NEATLOGS_API_KEY=<your existing key>
DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0
DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE=<pick-a-secret>
CODEX_API_KEY=<OpenAI API key>
```

- **`NEATLOGS_API_KEY`**: the line you already have; keep it as is. Without it the API still runs, but agent runs are not traced.
- **`DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0`**: makes the API reachable from outside the machine. Leave it out if you put Caddy in front, since Caddy reaches the API on loopback.
- **`DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE`**: any secret string you choose. Once set, the routes that reset the demo, inject faults, start investigations and approve repairs require it in an `X-Demo-Access-Code` header. Without it those routes are open to anyone with the URL.
- **`CODEX_API_KEY`**: only needed if you have not run `codex login` on the EC2 machine. Investigations use the Codex CLI and need one or the other.

You can leave the rest unset:

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `DTM_API_PORT` | `8000` |
| `DTM_POSTGRES_PORT` | `5432` |
| `DTM_AUTO_INVESTIGATE` | `0` (investigations start only when requested) |
| `DTM_INVESTIGATIONS_PER_HOUR` | `6` |
| `DTM_INVESTIGATIONS_PER_DAY` | `30` |

Leave the database URL and password settings alone: the defaults already match the Postgres container.

content.text:
**`DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE`** is a password for the API's write actions. The API has no login of its own, so once it listens on `0.0.0.0` anyone who reaches port 8000 can call every route, and `/docs` even gives them buttons to do it.

Setting the code makes these actions require it in an `X-Demo-Access-Code` header:

- **Start an investigation:** each one runs Codex under your signed-in account and uses your allowance (capped at 6 per hour and 30 per day by default).
- **Reset the demo:** wipes the demo data.
- **Inject faults and control traffic:** changes what the demo is doing.
- **Validate, approve, reject, apply and verify repairs:** changes the pipeline.

The read-only routes (health, incidents, metrics, alerts) stay open either way.

You only need it if port 8000 is open to everyone. If the security group rule for port 8000 has its source set to "My IP" rather than `0.0.0.0/0`, nobody else can reach the API and you can leave the code out.

**`CODEX_API_KEY`**: agreed, leave it out. Run `codex login` as `ec2-user`, the same user that runs the script, then confirm with `codex login status`, which is the check the backend itself uses. The EC2 machine has no browser, so the normal sign-in page can't open there; `codex login --device-auth` gives you a code to enter from your Mac's browser instead.

So your `.env` is just:

```
NEATLOGS_API_KEY=<your existing key>
DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0
```

Add `DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE=<pick-a-secret>` only if the port is open to the world.

That rule works: I just reached `http://ec2-54-198-163-191.compute-1.amazonaws.com:8000/api/health` from here and got a 200. It also means the API is open to the whole internet, so this is the case where you should set the access code.

On the EC2 machine:

```bash
printf '\nDTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE=%s\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" >> ~/dtm_build/.env
grep DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE ~/dtm_build/.env
./start-dtm-service.sh
```

The first line generates a random code and adds it to the file, the second prints it so you can copy it, and the third restarts the API with it. To use your own value instead, replace `$(openssl rand -hex 16)` with it.

After the restart, the write actions return 401 unless the code is supplied. In `/docs`, each of those routes has an `x-demo-access-code` field where you paste it.

If only you need access, the alternative is to change the rule's source from `0.0.0.0/0` to "My IP" and skip the code.

content.text:
No. People who only watch don't need it: all the read-only routes (incidents, metrics, alerts, pipeline runs, health) work without it.

The code is only for people who trigger actions: resetting the demo, injecting faults, starting investigations, or approving and applying repairs. So it depends on how you run the demo:

- **You drive, they watch:** keep the code to yourself.
- **They click through it themselves:** they need the code. Anyone you give it to can also spend your investigation allowance and reset the demo, so change it afterwards by editing `~/dtm_build/.env` and rerunning the script.

Because you deployed the backend only, viewers currently have just `/docs` and raw JSON to look at. If you later include the dashboard (`frontend/dist`) in the build, it has a field for entering the code and remembers it in the browser.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

# Rewrites on Vercel

A rewrite routes a request to a different destination without changing the URL in the browser. Unlike redirects, the user won't see the URL change.


<!-- docsgraph:related -->
## Related pages

> **For AI agents:** Follow these links to understand how this page connects to the rest of the Vercel ecosystem. For the full cross-link map (inbound, outbound, prerequisites, and semantic neighbors), see the .graph.md link below.

- [Vercel CDN now respects Cache-Control headers from external origins by default](https://vercel.com/changelog/vercels-cdn-now-respects-cache-control-headers-from-external-origins-by-default?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related)
- [How to enable CORS on Vercel](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/how-to-enable-cors?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Learn how to enable CORS on Vercel with vercel.json, Routing Middleware, framework config, and route handlers, plus how
- [Manage cache tags for external origins](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/how-to-manage-cache-tags-for-external-origins?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Learn how to use cache tags to optimally serve fresh content on Vercel when content from your external origin changes
- [Can I use Vercel as a reverse proxy?](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/vercel-reverse-proxy-rewrites-external?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Learn how to use rewrites to proxy requests from Vercel to other deployments.
- [rewrites](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/api-reference/config/next-config-js/rewrites?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Add rewrites to your Next.js app.
- [How can I increase the limit of redirects or use dynamic redirects on Vercel?](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/how-can-i-increase-the-limit-of-redirects-or-use-dynamic-redirects-on-vercel?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Instructions on how to use Serverless Functions to handle redirects on Vercel.
- [Using Vercel as a Standalone CDN](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/using_vercel_as_a_cdn?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related) — Use Vercel's external rewrites to proxy and cache content from external websites or APIs through Vercel's global edge ne
- [Redirects and rewrites now available in Observability](https://vercel.com/changelog/redirects-and-rewrites-now-available-in-observability?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=related)

Full cross-link map for this page: [/docs/routing/rewrites.graph.md](/docs/routing/rewrites.graph.md?from=related&source_path=%2Fdocs%2Frouting%2Frewrites&source_site=vercel-docs&relationship=graph)
<!-- /docsgraph:related -->

There are two main types:

1. **Same-application rewrites** – Route requests to different pages within your Vercel project.
2. **Rewrites to external origins** – Forward requests to an API or website outside your Vercel project.

The [/.well-known](# "The /.well-known directory") path is reserved and cannot be redirected or rewritten. Only
Enterprise teams can configure custom SSL. [Contact sales](/contact/sales) to
learn more.

## Setting up rewrites

Rewrites are defined in a `vercel.json` file in your project's root directory:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/source-path",
      "destination": "/destination-path"
    }
  ]
}
```

For all configuration options, see the [project configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#rewrites) docs.

## Same-application rewrites

Same-application rewrites route requests to different destinations within your project. Common uses include:

- **Friendly URLs**: Transform `/products/t-shirts` into `/catalog?category=t-shirts`
- **Device-specific content**: Show different layouts based on device type
- **A/B testing**: Route users to different versions of a page
- **Country-specific content**: Show region-specific content based on the user's location

Example: Route image resize requests to a serverless function:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/resize/:width/:height",
      "destination": "/api/sharp"
    }
  ]
}
```

This converts a request like `/resize/800/600` to `/api/sharp?width=800&height=600`.

Example: Route UK visitors to a UK-specific section:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/:path((?!uk/).*)",
      "has": [
        { "type": "header", "key": "x-vercel-ip-country", "value": "GB" }
      ],
      "destination": "/uk/:path*"
    }
  ]
}
```

This routes a UK visitor requesting `/about` to `/uk/about`.

## Rewrites to external origins

An external origin is any API or website outside your Vercel project. Rewrites to external origins forward requests to these destinations, effectively allowing Vercel to function as a reverse proxy or standalone CDN. You can use this feature to:

- **Proxy API requests**: Hide your actual API endpoint
- **Combine multiple services**: Merge multiple backends under one domain
- **Create microfrontends**: Combine multiple Vercel applications into a single website
- **Add caching**: Cache external API responses on the CDN
- **Serve externally hosted content**: Serve content that is not hosted on Vercel.

Example: Forward API requests to an external endpoint:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ]
}
```

A request to `/api/users` will be forwarded to `https://api.example.com/users` without changing the URL in the browser.

### Identifying the visitor at your origin

Vercel forwards [request headers](/docs/headers/request-headers) that identify the original visitor to your external origin. You don't need to add your own headers to pass this information along:

| Header                                                                   | Value                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`x-real-ip`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-real-ip)                   | The public IP address of the visitor                      |
| [`x-forwarded-for`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-for)       | The public IP address of the visitor                      |
| [`x-forwarded-host`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-host)     | The host the visitor requested, such as your domain       |
| [`x-forwarded-proto`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-proto)   | The protocol the visitor used, such as `https`            |

If your origin sits behind its own load balancer or proxy, configure it to trust these headers only for requests that come from Vercel. See [restricting your origin to Vercel traffic](#restricting-your-origin-to-vercel-traffic).

### Restricting your origin to Vercel traffic

When Vercel proxies traffic to your origin, you usually want the origin to reject requests that bypass Vercel and hit it directly. To do this, have Vercel attach a secret request header on every rewrite, then check that header at your origin.

1. Generate a long random value, for example with `openssl rand -hex 32`.

2. Add it to your project as an [environment variable](/docs/environment-variables), such as `ORIGIN_SECRET`.

3. Use a [`routes` transform](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#in-transforms) to set the header on requests that you rewrite to your origin:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
     "routes": [
       {
         "src": "/(.*)",
         "dest": "https://origin.example.com/$1",
         "transforms": [
           {
             "type": "request.headers",
             "op": "set",
             "target": {
               "key": "x-origin-secret"
             },
             "args": "$ORIGIN_SECRET",
             "env": ["ORIGIN_SECRET"]
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

4. At your origin or load balancer, reject any request where `x-origin-secret` doesn't match the expected value. Use a timing-safe comparison when you check the value in application code.

Because the `set` operation replaces any existing value, a visitor can't supply their own `x-origin-secret` header to get through. To rotate the secret, have your origin accept both the old and new values, update the environment variable, redeploy, and then remove the old value from your origin.

### Caching rewrites to external origins

Vercel honors `cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control` headers from upstream servers on external rewrites. When your upstream returns caching headers, Vercel caches the response on the CDN accordingly. This behavior is enabled by default for projects created on or after April 6, 2026, for older projects that have the setting enabled in the dashboard, or when you set the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header. Older projects retain the previous uncached behavior unless you [opt in](#honoring-cache-control-headers-for-older-projects).

> **💡 Note:** If your upstream returns caching headers you don't intend to honor, review them to ensure they reflect your intended caching strategy.

You can override upstream caching headers using [`CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) or [`Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) in your `vercel.json`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [
        {
          "key": "CDN-Cache-Control",
          "value": "max-age=60"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

This caches the response on the CDN for 60 seconds, regardless of what the upstream server returns.

> **💡 Note:** When caching external rewrites, it's best practice to also include a `Vercel-Cache-Tag` response header with a
> comma-separated list of tags so you can later [purge the CDN cache by tag](/docs/caching/cdn-cache/purge) at your convenience.

#### Disabling caching for rewrites to external origins

To opt out of the default caching behavior and prevent Vercel from caching upstream responses, set the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header to `0`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [
        { "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "0" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

This restores the previous behavior where upstream caching headers are ignored and responses are never cached.

For more information on caching headers, see the [Cache-Control headers documentation](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers).

### Honoring cache-control headers for older projects

> **💡 Note:** This section applies to projects created before April 6, 2026 that have not yet adopted the new default caching behavior. For projects created on or after April 6, 2026, external rewrites respect upstream `cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control` headers by default and this section does not apply.

Before April 6, 2026, external rewrites were not cached by default. To opt in to caching, you had to add the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header to your `vercel.json`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [{ "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "1" }]
    }
  ]
}
```

This tells Vercel to respect caching headers (`cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`) on the upstream response. Once enabled, you can control the cache duration in two ways:

1. **From your API (preferred)**: When you control the backend, return [`CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) or [`Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) headers in the API response:

   ```
   CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=60
   ```

   This caches the response on the CDN for 60 seconds.

2. **From Vercel configuration**: When you can't modify the backend, set caching headers in `vercel.json` alongside `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching`:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
     "rewrites": [
       {
         "source": "/api/:path*",
         "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
       }
     ],
     "headers": [
       {
         "source": "/api/:path*",
         "headers": [
           { "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "1" },
           {
             "key": "CDN-Cache-Control",
             "value": "max-age=60"
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

> comma-separated list of tags so you can later [purge the CDN cache by tag](/docs/caching/cdn-cache/purge) at your convenience.

You can export rewrite data by draining logs from your application. External origin events appear in your runtime logs, allowing you to monitor proxy requests, track external API calls, and analyze traffic patterns to your backend services.

You can observe your external origin performance using Observability. The **External Origins** tab shows request counts, connection latency, and traffic patterns for your proxied requests, helping you monitor backend performance and validate that rewrites are working as expected.

Learn more in the [Observability Insights](/docs/observability/insights#external-rewrites) documentation.

If your project uses [Services](/docs/services), a rewrite can target a service instead of a URL. Set `destination` to an object with a `service` key:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": { "service": "my_backend" }
    }
  ]
}
```

- **Astro**: [Astro routing](/docs/frameworks/frontend/astro#rewrites)
- **SvelteKit**: [SvelteKit routing](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/sveltekit#rewrites)

Use Vercel's preview deployments to test your rewrites before going to production. Each pull request creates a unique preview URL where you can verify your rewrites work correctly.

You can capture and forward parts of a path using wildcards:

```json
{

    {

    }
  ]
}
```

```json

    }
  ]
}
```

For more complex patterns, you can use regular expressions with capture groups:

```json
{
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "^/articles/(\\d{4})/(\\d{2})/(.+)$",
      "destination": "/archive?year=$1&month=$2&slug=$3"
    }
  ]
}
```

This converts `/articles/2023/05/hello-world` to `/archive?year=2023&month=05&slug=hello-world`.

You can also use named capture groups:

```json
{
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "^/products/(?<category>[a-z]+)/(?<id>\\d+)$",
      "destination": "/shop?category=$category&item=$id"
    }
  ]
}
```

This converts `/products/shirts/123` to `/shop?category=shirts&item=123`.

## When to use each type

- **Same-application rewrites**: Use when routing within your own application
- **Rewrites to external origins**: Use when connecting to external APIs, creating microfrontends, or using Vercel as a reverse proxy or standalone CDN for third-party content

There are two main types:

1. **Same-application rewrites** – Route requests to different pages within your Vercel project.
2. **Rewrites to external origins** – Forward requests to an API or website outside your Vercel project.

The [/.well-known](# "The /.well-known directory") path is reserved and cannot be redirected or rewritten. Only
Enterprise teams can configure custom SSL. [Contact sales](/contact/sales) to
learn more.

## Setting up rewrites

Rewrites are defined in a `vercel.json` file in your project's root directory:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/source-path",
      "destination": "/destination-path"
    }
  ]
}
```

For all configuration options, see the [project configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#rewrites) docs.

## Same-application rewrites

Same-application rewrites route requests to different destinations within your project. Common uses include:

- **Friendly URLs**: Transform `/products/t-shirts` into `/catalog?category=t-shirts`
- **Device-specific content**: Show different layouts based on device type
- **A/B testing**: Route users to different versions of a page
- **Country-specific content**: Show region-specific content based on the user's location

Example: Route image resize requests to a serverless function:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/resize/:width/:height",
      "destination": "/api/sharp"
    }
  ]
}
```

This converts a request like `/resize/800/600` to `/api/sharp?width=800&height=600`.

Example: Route UK visitors to a UK-specific section:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/:path((?!uk/).*)",
      "has": [
        { "type": "header", "key": "x-vercel-ip-country", "value": "GB" }
      ],
      "destination": "/uk/:path*"
    }
  ]
}
```

This routes a UK visitor requesting `/about` to `/uk/about`.

## Rewrites to external origins

An external origin is any API or website outside your Vercel project. Rewrites to external origins forward requests to these destinations, effectively allowing Vercel to function as a reverse proxy or standalone CDN. You can use this feature to:

- **Proxy API requests**: Hide your actual API endpoint
- **Combine multiple services**: Merge multiple backends under one domain
- **Create microfrontends**: Combine multiple Vercel applications into a single website
- **Add caching**: Cache external API responses on the CDN
- **Serve externally hosted content**: Serve content that is not hosted on Vercel.

Example: Forward API requests to an external endpoint:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ]
}
```

A request to `/api/users` will be forwarded to `https://api.example.com/users` without changing the URL in the browser.

### Identifying the visitor at your origin

Vercel forwards [request headers](/docs/headers/request-headers) that identify the original visitor to your external origin. You don't need to add your own headers to pass this information along:

| Header                                                                   | Value                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`x-real-ip`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-real-ip)                   | The public IP address of the visitor                      |
| [`x-forwarded-for`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-for)       | The public IP address of the visitor                      |
| [`x-forwarded-host`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-host)     | The host the visitor requested, such as your domain       |
| [`x-forwarded-proto`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-forwarded-proto)   | The protocol the visitor used, such as `https`            |

If your origin sits behind its own load balancer or proxy, configure it to trust these headers only for requests that come from Vercel. See [restricting your origin to Vercel traffic](#restricting-your-origin-to-vercel-traffic).

### Restricting your origin to Vercel traffic

When Vercel proxies traffic to your origin, you usually want the origin to reject requests that bypass Vercel and hit it directly. To do this, have Vercel attach a secret request header on every rewrite, then check that header at your origin.

1. Generate a long random value, for example with `openssl rand -hex 32`.

2. Add it to your project as an [environment variable](/docs/environment-variables), such as `ORIGIN_SECRET`.

3. Use a [`routes` transform](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#in-transforms) to set the header on requests that you rewrite to your origin:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
     "routes": [
       {
         "src": "/(.*)",
         "dest": "https://origin.example.com/$1",
         "transforms": [
           {
             "type": "request.headers",
             "op": "set",
             "target": {
               "key": "x-origin-secret"
             },
             "args": "$ORIGIN_SECRET",
             "env": ["ORIGIN_SECRET"]
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

4. At your origin or load balancer, reject any request where `x-origin-secret` doesn't match the expected value. Use a timing-safe comparison when you check the value in application code.

Because the `set` operation replaces any existing value, a visitor can't supply their own `x-origin-secret` header to get through. To rotate the secret, have your origin accept both the old and new values, update the environment variable, redeploy, and then remove the old value from your origin.

### Caching rewrites to external origins

Vercel honors `cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control` headers from upstream servers on external rewrites. When your upstream returns caching headers, Vercel caches the response on the CDN accordingly. This behavior is enabled by default for projects created on or after April 6, 2026, for older projects that have the setting enabled in the dashboard, or when you set the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header. Older projects retain the previous uncached behavior unless you [opt in](#honoring-cache-control-headers-for-older-projects).

> **💡 Note:** If your upstream returns caching headers you don't intend to honor, review them to ensure they reflect your intended caching strategy.

You can override upstream caching headers using [`CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) or [`Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) in your `vercel.json`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [
        {
          "key": "CDN-Cache-Control",
          "value": "max-age=60"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

This caches the response on the CDN for 60 seconds, regardless of what the upstream server returns.

> **💡 Note:** When caching external rewrites, it's best practice to also include a `Vercel-Cache-Tag` response header with a
> comma-separated list of tags so you can later [purge the CDN cache by tag](/docs/caching/cdn-cache/purge) at your convenience.

#### Disabling caching for rewrites to external origins

To opt out of the default caching behavior and prevent Vercel from caching upstream responses, set the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header to `0`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [
        { "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "0" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

This restores the previous behavior where upstream caching headers are ignored and responses are never cached.

For more information on caching headers, see the [Cache-Control headers documentation](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers).

### Honoring cache-control headers for older projects

> **💡 Note:** This section applies to projects created before April 6, 2026 that have not yet adopted the new default caching behavior. For projects created on or after April 6, 2026, external rewrites respect upstream `cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control` headers by default and this section does not apply.

Before April 6, 2026, external rewrites were not cached by default. To opt in to caching, you had to add the `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching` header to your `vercel.json`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "rewrites": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
    }
  ],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/api/:path*",
      "headers": [{ "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "1" }]
    }
  ]
}
```

This tells Vercel to respect caching headers (`cache-control`, `CDN-Cache-Control`, and `Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`) on the upstream response. Once enabled, you can control the cache duration in two ways:

1. **From your API (preferred)**: When you control the backend, return [`CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) or [`Vercel-CDN-Cache-Control`](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#cdn-cache-control-header) headers in the API response:

   ```
   CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=60
   ```

   This caches the response on the CDN for 60 seconds.

2. **From Vercel configuration**: When you can't modify the backend, set caching headers in `vercel.json` alongside `x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching`:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
     "rewrites": [
       {
         "source": "/api/:path*",
         "destination": "https://api.example.com/:path*"
       }
     ],
     "headers": [
       {
         "source": "/api/:path*",
         "headers": [
           { "key": "x-vercel-enable-rewrite-caching", "value": "1" },
           {
             "key": "CDN-Cache-Control",
             "value": "max-age=60"
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   This caches the response on the CDN for 60 seconds.

For more information on caching headers, see the [Cache-Control headers documentation](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers).

> **💡 Note:** When caching rewrites to external origins, it's best practice to also include a `Vercel-Cache-Tag` response header with a
> comma-separated list of tags so you can later [purge the CDN cache by tag](/docs/caching/cdn-cache/purge) at your convenience.

You can export rewrite data by draining logs from your application. External origin events appear in your runtime logs, allowing you to monitor proxy requests, track external API calls, and analyze traffic patterns to your backend services.

To get started, configure a [logs drain](/docs/drains/using-drains).

Learn more in the [Observability Insights](/docs/observability/insights#external-rewrites) documentation.

**What the sources do say**

Vercel's external rewrites are server-side. Vercel returns the backend's response under your domain, and the browser only sees requests to your domain. Vercel's own examples use HTTPS destinations, such as a request to /api/users forwarded to https://api.example.com/users. I couldn't find any official statement on whether an `http://` destination is accepted or how Vercel handles it.

**Likely cause (my reasoning, unverified)**

- If your frontend calls the API through a relative path like `/api/...` and the rewrite proxies it to `http://<ec2-ip>:8000`, the browser never makes an HTTP request, so mixed content shouldn't be the problem. Check whether the frontend still calls `http://<ec2-ip>:8000` directly, bypassing the rewrite. That is the most common cause of the error.
- If the browser does show a mixed-content error, the frontend is making an insecure request from an HTTPS page. Changing the rewrite alone won't fix that.
- Debug the proxy path first: check the EC2 security group allows inbound on 8000, confirm the app listens on 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1, and test `curl http://<ec2-ip>:8000/...` from outside AWS.

**Fixes**

1. Point the frontend at relative `/api` paths only, and keep the rewrite as the single entry point.
2. Serve the backend over HTTPS. Put nginx or Caddy on EC2 in front of port 8000 with a certificate for a domain, or use an AWS load balancer with an ACM certificate. Then set the rewrite destination to `https://api.yourdomain.com/:path*`. This is the more robust option.
3. Check CORS on the backend. A Korean developer's write-up described a similar setup where the backend's CORS relaxation was not applied to the build deployed on AWS. That was a different configuration, but it's worth ruling out.

If you can share the exact error text from the browser console and your `vercel.json`, I can narrow this down further.

I've checked how the frontend calls the API and added the Vercel config; here are the steps.

The frontend calls the API on its own address (`/api/...`), so the Vercel site has to forward those calls to the EC2 machine. I added [frontend/vercel.json](frontend/vercel.json) to do that: it forwards `/api/*` to `http://ec2-54-198-163-191.compute-1.amazonaws.com:8000/api/*` and turns off caching for those calls. This also gives you HTTPS without a domain, because the browser only ever talks to Vercel.

The frontend builds cleanly (I built it into a scratch folder, not your `dist`). I have not deployed anything. Vercel's docs only show `https://` destinations for this kind of forwarding and I couldn't confirm that a plain `http://` one is accepted, so step 4 is the real test.

## Steps

1. Sign in to Vercel from the frontend folder (this opens your browser):

   ```bash
   cd /Users/siddarth-ba-72/projects/DataTraceMind/frontend
   npx vercel login
   ```

2. Deploy to production:

   ```bash
   npx vercel --prod
   ```

3. Answer the first-run prompts:
   - **Set up and deploy?** Yes
   - **Link to existing project?** No
   - **Project name:** for example `datatracemind`
   - **In which directory is your code located?** `./`
   - **Modify the detected settings?** No (it detects Vite, builds with `npm run build` and serves `dist`)

4. Open `https://<your-project>.vercel.app/api/health`, using the address Vercel prints. You should see `{"status":"ok",...}`. If this fails, the forward to `http://` is being refused and the backend needs HTTPS first (the Caddy or CloudFront route from earlier).

5. Open the site itself: the incident console is at `/` and the Scenario Lab at `/lab/`. Both have a "Demo access code" field; paste your `DTM_DEMO_ACCESS_CODE` there to use the action buttons.

To redeploy after frontend changes, run `npx vercel --prod` again from the `frontend` folder.

## What must stay in place on the EC2 side

- **Port 8000 open to `0.0.0.0/0` and `DTM_API_HOST=0.0.0.0`:** Vercel's servers make the calls now, so you can't restrict the port to your own IP. Keep the access code set.
- **The EC2 address:** it is written into `vercel.json`. If the instance is stopped and started, the address changes and you need to update the file and redeploy; an Elastic IP avoids that.

Sources:
- [Rewrites on Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/routing/rewrites)

content.text:
Deploying from the dashboard means Vercel builds from your GitHub repo, so the config file has to be pushed first. Your `main` is otherwise in sync with GitHub; only `frontend/vercel.json` is missing there.

## 1. Push the config file

```bash
cd /Users/siddarth-ba-72/projects/DataTraceMind
git add frontend/vercel.json
git commit -m "Add Vercel config that forwards /api to the backend"
git push origin main
```

The repo is public, so the EC2 address in that file will be visible on GitHub.

## 2. Import the project in Vercel

1. Go to vercel.com, then **Add New… → Project**.
2. Under **Import Git Repository**, pick `siddarth-ba-72/DataTraceMind` and click **Import**. If it isn't listed, click **Adjust GitHub App Permissions** and grant access to that repo.
3. On the configure screen, enter:

   | Field | Value |
   |---|---|
   | Project Name | `datatracemind` (or any name) |
   | Root Directory | click **Edit** and select `frontend` |
   | Framework Preset | `Vite` (selected automatically once the root is set) |
   | Build Command | leave default (`npm run build`) |
   | Output Directory | leave default (`dist`) |
   | Install Command | leave default (`npm install`) |
   | Environment Variables | none |

4. Click **Deploy**.

The Root Directory is the one setting that matters: without it Vercel builds from the repo root and finds no frontend.

## 3. Check it

1. Open `https://<your-project>.vercel.app/api/health`. You should see `{"status":"ok",...}`, which proves the forward to the EC2 machine works.
2. Open `/` for the incident console and `/lab/` for the Scenario Lab, and paste your access code into the "Demo access code" field to use the action buttons.

If the health URL fails while the pages load, Vercel is refusing the plain `http://` forward and the backend needs HTTPS first.

After this, every push to `main` redeploys the site automatically.
